title: Puff pastry, full classical method
subtitle: Six to eight turns of folded butter for a pastry that rises to many visible layers
excerpt: Classical puff pastry is made by encasing a block of cold butter in a flour dough, then folding and rolling repeatedly to build hundreds of thin alternating layers. Baked in a hot oven, steam from the butter forces each layer apart. The result is the flakiest, most dramatically risen pastry in baking.
sourceNotes: Classical puff pastry lamination technique is documented in French patisserie tradition. The method of six to eight single turns creating 729 to 2187 layers is the standard professional baseline. Home adaptations with resting schedules are based on contemporary baking practice.

recipe.yieldDescription: About 650 g puff pastry (enough for a large pie top or 12 palmiers)
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the formed block after the final fold. Defrost overnight in the fridge before rolling to the final thickness.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The pastry improves with an overnight rest in the fridge. It can be refrigerated for up to 3 days before use.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven, very hot, fan 190°C; puff pastry needs an initial blast of heat to drive the layers apart

glossaryTerms.definition: The flour-and-water dough base in puff pastry, before the butter block is added. It is more elastic than shortcrust dough and is made with a small amount of fat to make it pliable without tearing.
The block of cold butter incorporated into the détrempe during lamination. It must be the same consistency as the détrempe when folded in, or it will break through the layers.

content.text: Classical puff pastry takes a day, requires cold conditions throughout, and rewards patience. The
encloses a block of cold butter (
), and six single folds build 729 alternating layers. Baked at high heat, steam pushes those layers apart.

250 g strong white flour, 5 g salt, 30 g cold unsalted butter (rubbed in), 150 ml cold water. Mix to a smooth, elastic dough. Score a cross in the surface, wrap, and rest in the fridge for 30 minutes.

Beat 200 g cold unsalted butter between two sheets of baking paper with a rolling pin until it forms a flat, even 15 cm square, about 1 cm thick. The butter should be pliable but still cold, ideally the same firmness as the détrempe. If it shatters when pressed, warm it briefly; if it is greasy and soft, chill it.

Roll the détrempe to a 30 cm square on a lightly floured surface. Place the butter block in the centre at a 45-degree angle (like a diamond on a square). Fold the four corners of the dough over the butter to enclose it completely. Press the seams firmly.

Roll the dough away from you to a rectangle roughly 60 × 20 cm. Fold the far third down and the near third up over it (like a business letter). This is one single fold. Give the dough a 90-degree turn, wrap, and rest in the fridge for 30 minutes. Repeat until you have completed six single folds in total, resting between each. Mark the turns so you do not lose count.

After the final rest, roll the pastry to the thickness required by the recipe (typically 3 to 5 mm for pies and tarts; 2 mm for palmiers and allumettes). Cut with a sharp knife or pastry wheel. Chill the cut shapes for 20 minutes before baking.

Puff pastry lives or dies on oven temperature. Domestic ovens drift by 20°C or more. An oven thermometer confirms the real temperature. At 210°C conventional, the layers should begin to separate within the first 5 minutes; if the pastry is browning without rising, the oven was too cool.
